title: Tail surge mitigation: streaming vs buffering deep dive
summary: Deep dive on p95/p99 tail behavior during policy-search surge. Covered differences between streaming and buffered (non-streaming) response modes, network hop contribution, KV cache hotkeys, batching strategies, and quantization trade-offs for Aurora's VPC deployment. Agreed to run a controlled 24-hour soak with synthetic surge and share dashboard + traces.

transcript:
--- Meeting Header ---
Date: 2026-03-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Claire N. (Redwood), Marcus L. (Redwood SE), Asha P. (Redwood SA), Priya K. (Aurora Head of Platform), Jamal W. (Aurora SRE), Elena S. (Aurora ML), Tom B. (Aurora CTO)
Recording ID: ff-20260328-aurora-td-07

Summary (auto): Deep technical session to isolate sources of tail latency during policy-search surge for Aurora Insurance. Focus on streaming vs buffered response modes, network hops, KV cache behavior, batching, and quantization.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Claire Nguyen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. um, we'll go through the p95/p99 behavior you saw in staging last week, and dig into streaming vs buffering strategies and where the tail actually comes from. Marcus, do you want to start with the observed numbers?
[00:18] Marcus Lee: Yeah, sure. So Aurora sent a sample trace last Friday, it showed median ~70ms but a p95 of 210ms and p99 spiking to 520ms during a brief 10-minute surge. That was with buffered responses (non-streaming) and 2 replicas behind the LB.
[00:36] Priya Kapoor: Right, and to add context, our users do a policy-lookup flow that fans out to 3 prompts in parallel and then we do a final ranking call, so bursts concentrate at about 1.2x normal QPS during peak times.
[00:51] Jamal Wright: We also observed that the p99 correlates with NAT gateway scaling events in our VPC - when a new NAT pair spins up, connections get rebalanced and some requests add an extra 30-80ms.
[01:07] Marcus Lee: That's a good callout. Network hops are often under-estimated in latency budgets. For the Redwood side we instrument at request ingress, kernel selection, kv cache checks, and token generation. The traces you sent show a few rows where the KV cache lookup was fine but the first token suffered a ~120ms wait.
[01:30] Elena Soto: Is that the "KV cash" you said earlier? sorry, I wrote kv cash in notes, clearly transcribe...
[01:36] Marcus Lee: (laughs) kv cache, yup. sometimes whispered as kv cash in the transcript.
[01:42] Tom Becker: Can you unpack streaming vs buffered for us? If we flip to streaming, does that change p99 significantly?
[01:50] Asha Patel: Short answer: sometimes yes, sometimes no. Streaming reduces tail impact from token-by-token generation because you start delivering earlier, but it can surface jitter if network hops add per-chunk latency. Buffered (non-streaming) can hide that jitter until finalization, so you might see worse p95/p99 at end but fewer incremental delays. There's also a CPU and context switching tradeoff on the server side for many concurrent streaming connections.
[02:18] Priya Kapoor: So streaming could make intermediate latencies visible to our frontend, but overall p99 for the end-to-end call might improve?
[02:25] Marcus Lee: Exactly. In our internal tests we saw streaming reduce p95 by ~20% in steady-state for 2-3 token chunk sizes, but when there's a network flake in the middle of a chunk, the perceived latency jumps for that user.
[02:41] Jamal Wright: Our firewall team asked about keepalives and TLS session reuse because we see session renegotiation during NAT rebalances. Does Redwood support long-lived connections from the VPC to reduce that?
[02:53] Claire Nguyen: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we recommend persistent connections and pinning to dedicated gateways. For your VPC setup, we can provide a private peering option to reduce NAT bounce and you can also use connection pooling at the LB layer.
[03:07] Elena Soto: On the ML side, how much does quantization change the tail distribution? We were worried that int8 or llama.cpp-like quant could increase variance.
[03:15] Marcus Lee: Good question. Quantization reduces median token latency because the kernel runs faster, but it can increase jitter in rare cases where fallback to higher precision happens (e.g., for custom ops or attention patterns). In our tests quantized fp8/int8 variants had a slightly higher p99 tail on very long sequences unless KV caching absorbed most of the repeated tokens.
[03:38] Priya Kapoor: Hmm ok. We run a lot of short prompts (average 24 tokens) with a few longer ranking calls. Would KV caching help more for the short ones or the ranking ones?
[03:47] Marcus Lee: KV caching helps for continuation/refixing patterns – so the ranking call that fans out then continues will benefit if you can cache the initial prefix. Short one-off queries less so. But there's a big win if you pre-warm the cache for the top N hot prefixes; that reduces both median and tail since cold starts are often the worst offenders.
[04:05] Jamal Wright: We're seeing hotkeying on two templates: "policy_search_v1" and "entity_expand_v2". Can Redwood automatically shard or TTL those keys differently?
[04:13] Asha Patel: We have config for key TTLs and hotkey isolation. For example, you can route heavy hitters to a small warm pool so they don't evict general cache entries. Also prefix partitioning helps. But if a single tenant floods one key you'll still see contention unless you apply per-key rate limits.
[04:31] Tom Becker: What about batching? Our instinct is to increase batch size to improve throughput, but we worry about added latency for small urgent calls.
[04:39] Marcus Lee: Dynamic batching with adaptive timeouts is the usual pattern: you set a max batch delay (say 8-12ms) and a max batch size. For latency-sensitive routes keep the timeout short and accept lower throughput. For backend ranking where throughput matters more you can increase window. Redwood Optimize can recommend per-route batch config based on your observed seq length distribution.
[05:00] Priya Kapoor: Any quick math you can show for effect on p99 if we go from batch delay 5ms to 15ms?
[05:07] Marcus Lee: Roughly, added batching delay is added to every request in the batch, so worst-case p99 can increase by that window. If your p99 was 520ms because of sporadic kernel scheduling, adding 10ms might be negligible. But if your baseline is tight, it can push you over SLOs. We'll produce a sensitivity spreadsheet.
[05:27] Claire Nguyen: (interruption) Also remember network hop + NAT jitter compounds with batching delay, so it's multiplicative in the tail.
[05:34] Jamal Wright: On instrumentation — the traces you sent were great but we need span-level breakdowns we can correlate with our VPC subnets. Can you attach span IDs to your traces?
[05:44] Marcus Lee: Yes we can include full span traces and also export them to your OTEL collector. We'll annotate the spans with kernel type, quantization variant, and cache hit/miss flags.
[05:56] Elena Soto: About streaming chunk sizes — you mentioned 2-3 token chunks earlier. Is there a sweet spot?
[06:02] Marcus Lee: Empirically 2-4 tokens per chunk balances start-of-response latency and network overhead. If you go 1 token chunks you pay more overhead per chunk; if you go >6 tokens you start to increase first-byte latency. Also chunking interacts with chunk reassembly on the client and your frontend timeouts.
[06:21] Tom Becker: If we enable streaming for the ranking flow, would that break any existing front-end logic?
[06:26] Priya Kapoor: Our frontend expects a single JSON response now. Switching to streaming would require changes to the aggregator to accept partials. That's non-trivial.
[06:33] Asha Patel: If changes are hard, consider hybrid: deliver a small 1-2 token preview stream to improve perceived latency while still finalizing a single JSON body at the end. That gives perceived snappiness without re-architecting too much.
[06:50] Jamal Wright: One specific concern: TLS renegotiation during NAT rebalancing caused a batch of requests to stall ~120-150ms. Would private peering eliminate that?
[06:59] Claire Nguyen: Private peering or a dedicated gateway eliminates the NAT hop and should remove that class of 30-150ms spikes. We recommend that for Dedicated customers with strict tail SLOs.
[07:12] Priya Kapoor: Great. Can you outline the concrete experiment? We want to see numbers for streaming vs buffered and q8 vs fp16.
[07:19] Marcus Lee: Proposed experiment — we'll run three variants across identical traffic: (A) buffered fp16, (B) buffered quantized (q8), (C) streaming fp16 with 3-token chunks. Each run 6 hours stable then 18 hours soak including synthetic 1.5x surge. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, top 50 slowest traces, and network hop counts.
[07:40] Tom Becker: Also make sure to include spike scenarios where we tear down a NAT and re-establish to simulate real infra churn.
[07:47] Asha Patel: We'll add that. Claire will share the benchmark doc and the orchestration playbook.
[07:52] Claire Nguyen: I'll drop links in the follow-up: perf spreadsheet (https://redwood.example/reports/aurora-p99), tracing dashboard sample, and a short runbook for peering.
[08:03] Priya Kapoor: Anything else on quantization safety? We need to be sure there are no regressions for our regulated policy text outputs.
[08:10] Marcus Lee: We'll include a quality eval set — ~200 prompts with golden outputs and measure rouge/bertscore and human-inspected diffs for top 20. If quantization shows >2% regression on critical prompts we won't recommend it for those routes.
[08:26] Jamal Wright: On the cache side, if we isolate hotkeys to a warm pool, what does that cost look like?
[08:33] Asha Patel: Cost depends on the size of warm pool and hit ratio. Warm pools are just reserved memory on the serving nodes; we can give an estimate after we see your prefix distribution.
[08:42] Elena Soto: Could you also include a run with pre-warming the cache for top 500 prefixes? We want to know cold-start impact.
[08:49] Marcus Lee: Yep, we'll include pre-warm vs no-prewarm in the plan.
[08:54] Tom Becker: Ok sounds actionable. Any blockers from Redwood side to run the tests in our staging VPC?
[09:00] Claire Nguyen: We'll need your staging network map and an API key for a dedicated test account. We'll also need permission to accept a small NAT peering for the duration if you want to test private connectivity.
[09:10] Priya Kapoor: We'll provide that by Tuesday.
[09:14] Claire Nguyen: Great. To recap: Redwood will run the 3-variant experiment, attach full spans to OTEL, include quant evals, and recommend batching/streaming configs. Aurora will provide topology, traceroutes, and approve staging connectivity. Follow-up on 2026-04-06.
[09:30] Jamal Wright: Thanks, that was super helpful.
[09:33] Claire Nguyen: Thanks everyone. I'll send the notes and the plan shortly.
[09:36] (call ends)
